title: India Blew Up the White House
description: Pokhran-II (Operation Shakti), May 1998: how India hid its nuclear tests from US spy satellites.

narration.style: highly expressive, gripping storyteller for a viral YouTube Short about a true heist

lines.text: India blew up the White House.
And America only found out when India announced it.
Not that White House.
A shaft in the Rajasthan desert,
two hundred metres deep,
code-named White House.
With a hydrogen bomb inside.
Rewind to 1995.
Imagine you're India's nuclear team, getting ready to test right here.
But American spy satellites are watching.
The New York Times prints it.
The US ambassador shows up with the photos.
President Clinton calls your Prime Minister.
Test cancelled.
Now it's 1998.
A new Prime Minister, Atal Bihari Vajpayee, gives the order: do it again.
Same desert. Same satellites.
But this time, they must see nothing.
So you work only at night.
And by sunrise, every truck is back in its exact parking spot,
so the morning photos look the same.
The sand you dig out? Shaped by hand into dunes, the way the wind would make them.
The shafts hide under camouflage nets.
When a satellite passes overhead,
work stops.
In between, the soldiers play cricket,
so the pictures show a bored army camp.
Your scientists arrive dressed as soldiers.
Even India's missile man, Abdul Kalam, gets a fake army name: Prithviraj.
The bombs arrive at dawn: flown in from Mumbai on an air force plane,
then driven into the desert by an army convoy.
Three go down into the shafts.
Code names: White House,
Taj Mahal,
and Kumbhkaran.
May 11th. Everything is set for nine a.m.
Then the wind blows the wrong way.
If anything leaks, it must not drift toward people.
So the most secret team in India just waits.
Six hours. Staring at the wind.
At three forty-five p.m., the wind turns.
The key turns.
The desert jumps.
In Khetolai, the nearest village, people say their walls cracked.
Hours later, Vajpayee walks out to the cameras:
Today, at fifteen forty-five hours, India conducted three underground nuclear tests in the Pokhran range.
In Washington, the phones start ringing.
America's spies had missed the whole thing.
A US senator calls it a colossal failure.
The CIA's own review finds it simply assumed India would never test.
Two days later, you test two more.
On May 27th, Vajpayee tells Parliament: India is now a nuclear weapon state.
Four years later, the scientist with the fake army name,
the one the satellites never noticed,
becomes the President of India.
And every May 11th, India celebrates National Technology Day.
All because of one afternoon in the desert,
when India blew up the White House.

paper.folio: THE NEW YORK TIMES, FRIDAY, DECEMBER 15, 1995
headline: U.S. Suspects India
Prepares To Conduct
Nuclear Test
